title: Delhi
selection: Delhi recorded an estimated 1.999 million foreign tourist visits in 2024 (India Tourism Data Compendium 2025, Table 4.1.2) and is the busiest international gateway for arrivals from Europe and the Americas. It has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites; Qutub Minar (220,044), Humayun's Tomb (158,043) and Red Fort (79,311) are among the ten ASI monuments most visited by foreign visitors in FY 2024-25 (Table 4.2.2).

places.name: Delhi
places.summary: India's capital: three World Heritage Sites, Old Delhi's bazaars and street food, and the country's busiest international gateway.
places.seoTitle: Delhi Travel Guide: Red Fort, Qutub Minar & Old Delhi
places.seoDescription: Plan your Delhi trip: Red Fort, Qutub Minar and Humayun's Tomb, Old Delhi food, metro and airport transfers, best season, air quality and practical tips.

images.commons: File:Front view with a clear blue sky of Humayun's Tomb.jpg
images.alt: The red sandstone and white marble Humayun's Tomb under a clear blue sky in Delhi
images.caption: Humayun's Tomb, Delhi

overview.text:
India's capital is one of its oldest cities. The Ministry of Tourism counts eight historic cities within it, each built over the ruins of the last, and three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Shah Jahan's Red Fort, the 12th-century Qutub Minar and Humayun's Tomb, the garden mausoleum that inspired the Taj Mahal.

For most international travellers Delhi is also the start of the trip: Indira Gandhi International has been India's busiest airport since 2009, and the city is the first stop on the classic Golden Triangle with Agra and Jaipur. Give it at least two days. Spend one in Old Delhi — the Red Fort, the Jama Masjid and the lanes of Chandni Chowk — and one in New Delhi and the south, from Humayun's Tomb and India Gate to the Qutub complex.

Timing matters here more than in most cities. October to March is the comfortable season, summers are very hot, and winter brings fog and, often, heavy smog. Several big sights close one day a week, so check the visiting information below before you fix your days.

items.body: Red Fort: Shah Jahan's palace-fortress, home to the Mughal emperors for almost 200 years (closed Mondays).
Qutub Minar: the 72.5 m tower begun in 1199, surrounded by the ruins of Delhi's first mosque.
Humayun's Tomb: the first garden tomb on the subcontinent, and the model for the Taj Mahal.
Chandni Chowk: Old Delhi's spice markets, jewellers' lanes and street food.
Gurudwara Bangla Sahib: free langar served to thousands every day, open around the clock.
Spend a day in Old Delhi: the Red Fort, the Jama Masjid's southern minaret and the spice market at Khari Baoli.
See the Mughal and Sultanate monuments: Humayun's Tomb in the morning and the Qutub complex in the late afternoon.
Shop the markets — Connaught Place, Chandni Chowk, Lajpat Nagar, Khan Market and Sarojini Nagar — or buy crafts from across India at Dilli Haat.
Eat your way through Chandni Chowk's street food and sweets.
Watch the evening sound and light show at the Red Fort (not on Mondays).

best_time.text:
October to March is the season the Ministry of Tourism recommends, and it is the most comfortable time for walking around monuments. Summer starts in April and peaks in late May or early June, when heat waves are common. The monsoon arrives in late June and lasts until mid-September.

Winter has its own catch. Dense fog is common, and in the World Air Quality Report 2024 Delhi was the world's most polluted capital, with smog made worse by crop burning in neighbouring states. If you are sensitive to air pollution, check the daily air-quality index before planning a day outdoors, and consider November and December the riskiest months.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: Indira Gandhi International Airport is India's busiest and the main gateway for international visitors. The Airport Express metro line runs from the airport to New Delhi station in about 15 minutes.

By train: Delhi has five main stations — New Delhi, Old Delhi, Hazrat Nizamuddin, Anand Vihar Terminal and Sarai Rohilla. Check which one your train uses. New Delhi station sits next to Paharganj, about 2 km north of Connaught Place. Book tickets on IRCTC.

local_transport.text: The Delhi Metro is the easiest way to cover long distances: it connects most of the city and nearby towns, and the first coach of every train is reserved for women. For Old Delhi, take the metro to the edge of the old city, then walk or hire a cycle rickshaw through the lanes. Auto-rickshaws and app-based taxis fill the gaps — agree the fare or use the meter before you set off.

where_to_stay.text: Paharganj, beside New Delhi station, is the traditional budget area and convenient for early trains. Connaught Place, about 2 km south, puts you at the centre of the metro network with plenty of restaurants. Many mid-range and upscale hotels are in South Delhi, which is calmer but further from Old Delhi. If you have an early flight, a hotel near the airport line saves time.

items.body: Delhi classics: butter chicken, dal makhani, chole bhature, dahi bhalla and chaat — Delhi is also where Mughlai cuisine originated.
Chandni Chowk for street food, sweets and spices — go hungry.
Langar (a free communal meal) at Gurudwara Bangla Sahib, open to everyone.
At mosques, temples and gurdwaras, dress modestly, remove your shoes and cover your head where asked (head scarves are usually provided at gurdwaras).
Akshardham doesn't allow phones or cameras inside — leave them at the cloakroom.
At the Lotus Temple, keep silence inside the prayer hall.
Ask before photographing people, especially at places of worship.

items.title: Visas
items.body: Apply for an e-Tourist visa at least 4 days before you arrive; your passport needs at least six months' validity.

items.title: Payments
items.body: Visitors can pay by QR code with NPCI's UPI One World wallet after a passport-and-visa KYC check. Carry some cash for markets and rickshaws.

items.title: Weekly closures
items.body: The Red Fort and Akshardham close on Mondays — plan Old Delhi or Humayun's Tomb for that day.

items.title: Monument tickets
items.body: Check current fees and buy tickets for ASI monuments on the Archaeological Survey of India's official site before you go.

items.title: Emergency
items.body: Dial 112 for police, fire or ambulance anywhere in India.

items.title: Air quality
items.body: In winter, check the air-quality index daily; people with asthma or heart conditions should limit time outdoors on smoggy days.

items.title: Heat
items.body: From April to June, sightsee early and late, carry water and rest indoors at midday.

items.title: Crowds
items.body: Old Delhi's markets are crowded — keep valuables zipped away.

items.title: Which Delhi sights close on Mondays?
items.body: The Red Fort and Akshardham are closed on Mondays. Humayun's Tomb and the Qutub Minar open daily from sunrise to sunset.

items.title: How do I get from the airport to the city?
items.body: The Airport Express metro line reaches New Delhi station in about 15 minutes; taxis are the alternative.

items.title: When is the best time to visit Delhi?
items.body: October to March. Summers are very hot, the monsoon runs from late June to mid-September, and winter smog can be severe.

items.title: How many days do I need?
items.body: Two full days cover Old Delhi and the main monuments of New Delhi and the south.
Group sights by area: Old Delhi (Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Chandni Chowk) in one day, New Delhi and the south in another.
Use the metro to beat road traffic between areas.
Don't plan the Red Fort on a Monday.

overview.text:
In 1639 the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan moved his court from Agra to Delhi and ordered a new palace-fortress at the heart of his new city, Shahjahanabad. The Red Fort, named for its red sandstone walls, was the residence of the Mughal emperors for almost 200 years, and the Red Fort Complex became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007.

Visits begin at the Lahori Gate and pass through the covered Meena Bazaar to the Naubat Khana, now the Indian War Memorial Museum, and on to the Diwan-i-Am and the marble pavilions of the private palaces. The Mumtaz Mahal houses the Red Fort Archaeological Museum. The fort still matters to modern India: every Independence Day the Prime Minister raises the national flag here. In 2024–25 it drew 2.88 million domestic visitors, the fourth most of any ticketed ASI monument.

overview.text:
Standing 72.5 m high, the Qutub Minar is the tallest masonry tower in India. Qutb-ud-din Aibak, founder of the Delhi Sultanate, began it in 1199 and completed the first storey; his successor Iltutmish added three more. Built of red and buff sandstone and covered in carved bands of inscriptions, it is the centrepiece of the Qutb complex, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993.

Give yourself time for the rest of the complex: the Quwwat ul-Islam Mosque, the Alai Darwaza gateway, the unfinished Alai Minar and the tombs of Iltutmish and Alauddin Khalji. In the courtyard, the Iron Pillar carries a 4th-century Sanskrit inscription in Brahmi script. In 2024 the Qutub Minar was India's third most visited ticketed monument for both Indian and foreign visitors.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Sunrise to sunset; timings may vary with the season.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: Check the current fee on the Archaeological Survey of India's official site before you go.
Go in the late afternoon for warm light on the sandstone.
Allow 1.5–2 hours to see the whole complex, not just the tower.

overview.text:
Humayun's Tomb was commissioned in 1558 by Empress Bega Begum, Humayun's first wife, and built by Persian architects with Indian craftsmen. It was the first garden tomb on the Indian subcontinent, set in a four-part charbagh garden, and its design inspired later Mughal tombs, culminating in the Taj Mahal. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993.

The complex is sometimes called the necropolis of the Mughals: more than 100 graves lie within it. Before the main tomb you pass Isa Khan's tomb, which predates Humayun's, and the blue-tiled Nila Gumbad. The tomb is in Nizamuddin East, near Purana Qila, and the Nizamuddin Dargah and Sunder Nursery are a short walk away. In 2024–25 it received 158,043 foreign visitors, the fourth most of any ticketed ASI monument.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Sunrise to sunset.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: Check the current fee on the Archaeological Survey of India's official site before you go.
Combine with Sunder Nursery next door and the qawwali at Nizamuddin Dargah.
Early morning is quietest and best for photographs.

places.name: Jama Masjid
places.summary: Shah Jahan's great mosque in Old Delhi, with a courtyard for 25,000 worshippers and minaret views over the old city.
places.seoTitle: Jama Masjid Delhi: Timings, Etiquette & Minaret Views
places.seoDescription: Visit the Jama Masjid in Old Delhi, one of India's largest mosques: history, visiting hours, dress and etiquette, and the climb up the southern minaret.

images.alt: The red sandstone courtyard and gateway of the Jama Masjid in Delhi with visitors
images.caption: The courtyard of the Jama Masjid

overview.text:
The Jama Masjid was built by Shah Jahan between 1650 and 1656 at the highest point of his new city, Shahjahanabad, and remains one of the largest mosques in India. Its red sandstone and marble courtyard can hold up to 25,000 worshippers, and it is still an active place of prayer.

For the best view of Old Delhi, climb the southern minaret. The mosque is a short walk from the Red Fort and the lanes of Chandni Chowk, so it fits easily into a day in the old city. Avoid prayer times, especially Friday midday prayers, when the mosque is busiest with worshippers.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 7 am – 12 pm and 1:30 pm – 6:30 pm.

items.title: Dress
items.body: Cover shoulders and legs and remove your shoes before entering.
Visit after the Red Fort, then walk into Chandni Chowk for lunch.

places.name: Chandni Chowk
places.summary: Shah Jahan's 17th-century boulevard, now Old Delhi's busiest market: spices, jewellery, sweets and street food.
places.seoTitle: Chandni Chowk, Old Delhi: Markets & Street Food Guide
places.seoDescription: Explore Chandni Chowk in Old Delhi: Khari Baoli spice market, Dariba Kalan's jewellers, Mughlai food and street food, and how to get around the lanes.

images.commons: File:Chandni Chowk, Old Delhi, India - September 2014.jpg
images.alt: Rickshaws and traffic beside the Chandni Chowk street sign in Old Delhi
images.caption: Chandni Chowk, Old Delhi

overview.text:
Chandni Chowk was laid out in the 17th century by Shah Jahan as the grand boulevard of his new capital; its name means 'Moonlight Square', after a pool that once reflected the moon. Today it is the crowded, noisy heart of Old Delhi and one of the city's great experiences.

Each lane has its own trade. Khari Baoli is Asia's largest wholesale spice market; Dariba Kalan, once the street of jewellers, still sells silver, pearls and ittar (natural perfume). Food is the other reason to come — from long-established Mughlai restaurants to street food and sweets. Go with time and an appetite, and see it on foot or by cycle rickshaw.

items.body: Mornings are calmer; many shops open late morning.
Take the metro to the old city rather than driving — roads here are slow.
Keep bags closed and valuables out of sight in the crowds.

places.name: India Gate
places.summary: Lutyens's 42 m war memorial arch on Kartavya Path, a favourite place for an evening walk.
places.seoTitle: India Gate Delhi: History, Visiting Hours & Nearby Sights
places.seoDescription: Visit India Gate in New Delhi, the war memorial designed by Lutyens: its history, when to go, evening lights and nearby sights like the National War Memorial.

images.commons: File:India Gate, New Delhi from West.jpg
images.alt: The sandstone arch of India Gate seen across the lawns from the west, New Delhi
images.caption: India Gate from the west

overview.text:
India Gate is a 42 m sandstone arch designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens as a memorial to the 70,000 Indian soldiers who died in the First World War and the Third Anglo-Afghan War. The Duke of Connaught laid the foundation stone in 1921, and the Viceroy, Lord Irwin, dedicated it in 1931.

It stands on Kartavya Path, the ceremonial avenue where the Republic Day parade is held each January. The surrounding lawns are open all day and popular with families in the evening, when the arch is lit up, though some areas close after dark. The National War Memorial is a short walk away.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Open throughout the day; some areas are closed to visitors after dark.

items.title: Entry
items.body: No ticket is needed to walk around the lawns.

places.name: Lotus Temple
places.summary: Delhi's Bahá'í House of Worship: 27 marble petals around a silent prayer hall open to people of every faith.
places.seoTitle: Lotus Temple Delhi: Timings, Etiquette & Architecture
places.seoDescription: Visit the Lotus Temple, Delhi's Bahá'í House of Worship: opening hours in summer and winter, silence in the prayer hall, and its 27-petal marble design.

images.alt: The white marble petals of the Lotus Temple above its blue reflecting pools in Delhi
images.caption: The Lotus Temple

overview.text:
The Lotus Temple is a Bahá'í House of Worship that opened in December 1986. As at every Bahá'í temple, anyone may enter regardless of religion. Its shape is unmistakable: 27 free-standing marble petals in clusters of three, with nine doors leading into a central hall for up to 2,500 people, surrounded by nine reflecting pools.

Inside there are no idols or sermons. At set times there are readings from the sacred texts of many faiths; at other times visitors may pray or meditate in silence. Expect a short queue at busy times, and keep your voice down in the hall.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 9:30 am – 7 pm in summer; 9:30 am – 5:30 pm in winter.

items.title: Inside
items.body: Silence in the prayer hall; shoes are removed before entering.

places.name: Swaminarayan Akshardham
places.summary: A vast marble and sandstone temple complex in east Delhi with exhibitions and an evening water show — no phones allowed.
places.seoTitle: Akshardham Temple Delhi: Timings, Rules & What to See
places.seoDescription: Visit Swaminarayan Akshardham in Delhi: opening hours and Monday closure, the no-phone rule, the boat ride, the evening water show and how to get there by metro.

overview.text: Swaminarayan Akshardham is a huge temple complex dedicated to Bhagwan Swaminarayan, built of Italian Carrara marble and pink sandstone. Beyond the temple itself there is a boat ride through Indian history, the Hall of Values exhibition and, after dark, the Sahaj Anand Water Show. It is about half a kilometre from Akshardham metro station. Phones and cameras are not allowed inside, and it is closed on Mondays.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 9:30 am – 6:30 pm, Tuesday to Sunday. Closed on Mondays.

items.title: Electronics
items.body: Leave phones, cameras and other electronic devices at the designated area before entering.

items.title: Getting there
items.body: About 500 m from Akshardham metro station.

places.name: Gurudwara Bangla Sahib
places.summary: Central Delhi's best-known Sikh gurdwara, with a sacred pool and a free community kitchen open to everyone.
places.seoTitle: Gurudwara Bangla Sahib Delhi: Langar, Etiquette & Timings
places.seoDescription: Visit Gurudwara Bangla Sahib in central Delhi: its history, the free langar served daily, the sarovar, etiquette for visitors and opening hours.

images.alt: The white gurdwara with a golden dome reflected in the sarovar at Gurudwara Bangla Sahib
images.caption: The sarovar at Gurudwara Bangla Sahib

overview.text:
Gurudwara Bangla Sahib stands on the site of a palace belonging to Raja Jai Singh, where the eighth Sikh Guru, Guru Har Krishan, stayed in 1664 and cared for the sick during an epidemic. Today its white marble building and golden domes rise above a large sarovar, or sacred pool.

The gurdwara welcomes visitors of every faith around the clock. In the langar hall, volunteers serve free meals to thousands of people every day, whatever their caste, creed or status — sitting down to eat together is the best way to understand the Sikh principle of equality. Cover your head, remove your shoes and wash your feet before entering.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Open 24 hours.

items.title: Etiquette
items.body: Cover your head (scarves are available), remove your shoes and don't bring tobacco or alcohol.

itineraries.title: Two days in Delhi: Old Delhi and the Mughal monuments
itineraries.summary: Day one in Old Delhi — the Red Fort, Jama Masjid and Chandni Chowk; day two from Humayun's Tomb to India Gate and the Qutub Minar.
itineraries.seoTitle: 2 Days in Delhi Itinerary: Old Delhi to Qutub Minar
itineraries.seoDescription: A realistic two-day Delhi itinerary: the Red Fort, Jama Masjid and Chandni Chowk, then Humayun's Tomb, India Gate and the Qutub Minar, with metro tips and timings.

plan.overview: Delhi is spread out and its traffic is slow, so this plan groups sights by area and uses the metro between them. Day 1 covers Old Delhi; Day 2 covers the Mughal and colonial monuments of New Delhi and the south. Don't start on a Monday: the Red Fort is closed that day — swap the days if you need to.

days.title: Old Delhi
days.summary: Shah Jahan's city: the fort, the great mosque and the market lanes between them.

stops.name: Red Fort
stops.note: Opens at 9:30 am; closed Mondays. Enter by the Lahori Gate.

stops.name: Jama Masjid
stops.note: Closed to visitors 12–1:30 pm; climb the southern minaret for the view.

stops.name: Chandni Chowk
stops.note: Lunch on Old Delhi food, then walk or take a cycle rickshaw to Khari Baoli and Dariba Kalan.

stops.name: Gurudwara Bangla Sahib
stops.note: Open 24 hours; join the langar if you like.

days.travel: The Red Fort, Jama Masjid and Chandni Chowk are within walking distance of each other. Take a metro or taxi to Bangla Sahib in central Delhi.
days.meals: Street food or a Mughlai lunch in Chandni Chowk; langar at Bangla Sahib.

days.title: New Delhi and the Qutub Minar
days.summary: From the first Mughal garden tomb to the Delhi Sultanate's victory tower.

stops.name: Humayun's Tomb
stops.note: Opens at sunrise; mornings are quietest.

stops.name: India Gate
stops.note: Walk the lawns; the National War Memorial is close by.

stops.name: Qutub Minar
stops.note: Stay until closing for warm light on the sandstone.

days.travel: Taxi or auto-rickshaw between stops, or the metro to the Qutub Minar (road times depend heavily on traffic — allow 30–60 minutes per leg as an estimate).
days.meals: Lunch in Connaught Place or Khan Market; try butter chicken or dal makhani for dinner.

budget.assumptions: Entry fees for the ASI monuments (Red Fort, Humayun's Tomb, Qutub Minar) change, so check them on the Archaeological Survey of India's official site. Jama Masjid, Chandni Chowk, India Gate and Bangla Sahib have no entry ticket. Accommodation, transport and meals vary too widely to estimate here.

lines.label: Red Fort, Humayun's Tomb, Qutub Minar
lines.basis: Not estimated — official fee pages couldn't be confirmed

lines.label: India Gate, Chandni Chowk, Bangla Sahib
lines.basis: Open public spaces and places of worship

booking.detail: Buy online on the ASI's official site to skip the ticket queue.
Book on IRCTC and check which of Delhi's five main stations your train uses.

alternatives: On a Monday, swap the days — the Red Fort is closed.
Replace the Qutub Minar with the Lotus Temple (closes earlier in winter) or Akshardham (closed Mondays, no phones).
Smoggy day? Spend more time indoors at the Red Fort museums or the National Museum.
tips: Use the metro between areas to avoid traffic.
Carry a scarf for the mosque and the gurdwara.
